agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 is the superscription, which the KJV leaves unnumbered (41:0); every later verse is one ahead of the KJV.

Malbim's explanation of 'eats my bread' as the royal food-taster is a late rationalization and I did not use it. I did not trace the psalm to a particular event in David's life. John 13:18 quotes this verse, and I left it out of the commentary because it is outside the text and the packet.

agent_notes: Revised after review. Radak's reading of va'ashallemah is that the repayment is withholding sympathy: no sackcloth in their illness, no prayer for them. He also cites 'the Gaon' (Saadia) for good in return for evil, tied to Ps 35:13. Radak, citing Ps 7:5, rules out harm to them. The simpler 'requite, punish' of the KJV and BBE is the other main reading, and Meiri and Metzudat David lean to it (Metzudat David: 'according to their deeds'). I kept the verb open in the literal layer and let the commentary lay out both.

agent_notes: Revised after review. The literal layer now reads 'Blessed [is] YHWH', matching the note: baruch is a passive participle with no verb in the Hebrew. I no longer call the KJV's 'be' an error; it reads the line as a wish where the Hebrew leaves wish and declaration open. STEPBible's '[be] blessed' was changed for consistency.

agent_notes: dal is glossed 'the weak one' rather than 'the poor'. Rashi and Radak read it as 'sick' (2 Sam 13:4), Metzudat David and Malbim as 'poor'. The Hebrew keeps both senses open, and the psalm goes on to a sickbed.
Qere/Ketiv: the Ketiv is written with yod (yeushshar, 'he will be called blessed'), the Qere is ve'ushshar with waw, as Radak notes. I glossed the Qere and treated the sense as the same.

Ibn Ezra says the verbs of vv. 2-4 may be prayer as well as promise, and Radak says the same for the jussive-looking 'al titteNehu. I rendered them as statements of confidence and flagged the second-person shift in the commentary.

Revised after review. The nurse reading (turning the sick person from side to side) is attributed to Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David only. Radak's first reading is that the bed, meant for rest, has been turned into suffering; Meiri reads it the same way. Radak's prayer reading (hafakhta as 'turn!') is kept as the alternative. The KJV 'make all his bed' is kept out of the literal layer because hafakh is 'turn, overturn'.

agent_notes: The phrase devar-beliya'al yatzuq bo is disputed: a 'worthless thing' (a deed, a curse, or a disease) 'is poured out' on him. Rashi and Metzudat David take it as his own sin; Radak offers 'a grave disease clings'. I kept 'a thing of worthlessness' in the literal line and chose 'a worthless thing, a curse' for the drama.
